poster.title: The Secret in Their Eyes
poster.creator: Poster artist uncredited
poster.edition: Spanish-language theatrical poster for the 2009 Argentine film
poster.alt: El secreto de sus ojos poster with three characters against a golden station interior, a red jacket near the centre and a white title across the dark lower half.
poster.blurb: A station’s depth connects three figures who look in different directions.

notes.title: A corridor pulls the eye inward
notes.body: The bright station interior recedes between the large foreground faces. Its perspective gives the flat montage a deep central passage.

notes.title: One red interruption
notes.body: The woman’s red jacket breaks the otherwise muted gold and black palette. That compact warm accent helps locate her between the larger male portraits.

notes.title: The title emerges from shadow
notes.body: Large white words sit over the dark lower half, where image details nearly disappear. Their contrast lets the faces and the name remain separate reading stages.

poster.reproduction: Poster for Juan José Campanella’s 2009 film, with Ricardo Darín, Soledad Villamil and Guillermo Francella. It is not the 2015 English-language remake. The small source reproduction is retained without enlargement.
poster.posterDateStatus: 2009 film campaign; precise printing date unverified.

studyData.intro: Three faces stand within a station that seems to recede far behind them. Follow the competing gazes and changes of scale, then separate the Spanish title, campaign promise and film context.

regions.label: Left foreground face
regions.summary: A large, sharply lit face opens the composition.

sections.heading: Close enough to read detail
sections.body: The left face is the largest and most forward-looking portrait. Light picks out the brow, nose and cheek while the beard forms a darker lower boundary. Its scale makes individual facial marks more accessible than the tiny people in the station behind it.

sections.heading: A named protagonist
sections.body: Sony Pictures Classics identifies Ricardo Darín as Benjamín Espósito, a retired investigator who revisits an unresolved case while writing a novel. That film context helps orient the portrait. The exact emotion or moment represented by this publicity image is not established by the synopsis.

regions.question: What is the first facial detail you notice before learning the character’s name?

regions.label: Suit and white collar
regions.summary: A dark triangular body supports the large face.

sections.heading: A wide base beneath a head
sections.body: The foreground jacket extends across much of the lower image, with a pale collar and narrow dark tie. Its shoulders create sloping edges toward the centre and left boundary. The suit makes the face feel physically grounded within an otherwise assembled publicity composition.

sections.heading: Clothes as shape first
sections.body: A suit can suggest a formal setting, but it does not independently establish a job or social rank. Here the useful visible evidence is the contrast between dark fabric, white collar and warm skin, and the way those shapes frame the face.

regions.question: Which part of the collar most strongly draws your eye back toward the face?

regions.label: Central woman
regions.summary: A smaller frontal figure stands inside the station’s light.

sections.heading: A central interruption
sections.body: The woman’s dark hair and red jacket interrupt the golden background. Her head sits between the two men, while her body occupies the station’s bright opening. She is smaller than the foreground man but gains attention through colour and central placement.

sections.heading: More than a supporting shape
sections.body: The distributor identifies Soledad Villamil as Irene, Espósito’s former colleague and an important part of his remembered and present life. That relationship belongs to the film’s story. The poster’s placement alone cannot tell us how much narrative agency any character has.

regions.question: Does colour or central placement do more to make this figure noticeable?

regions.label: Red patterned jacket
regions.summary: A warm colour differs from the men’s dark clothes.

sections.heading: Pattern within a colour accent
sections.body: The jacket is red with darker surface marks rather than a uniform flat patch. Its open neckline produces a narrow pale triangle. These details make it distinct from both the dark suits and the broad golden architectural shapes behind it.

sections.heading: A controlled difference
sections.body: The red helps separate this body from the surrounding yellow-green light, even though both are warm in comparison with the black lower field. Compare colour and edge together: the jacket would still be distinguishable in greyscale, but by different cues.

regions.question: Try imagining the jacket grey. What would still separate it from the station?

regions.label: Seated man at right
regions.summary: A tilted head and glasses turn attention inward.

sections.heading: A different posture
sections.body: The right-hand man leans back and turns his head toward the centre. His glasses introduce two angular frames near the eyes. The pale shirt and diagonal jacket opening echo the foreground collar, while his smaller scale keeps him from matching the left portrait’s dominance.

sections.heading: A triangle of attention
sections.body: The three heads form an uneven triangle. Their orientations do not resolve into a simple exchange of eye contact, which can leave the viewer searching for a relationship. The arrangement invites comparison without proving that the figures share one literal scene.

regions.question: Can you follow a complete chain of eye contact among the three people?

regions.label: Golden station depth
regions.summary: Architecture leads from the foreground toward a bright distance.

sections.heading: A depth behind the portraits
sections.body: Curved roof structures and converging edges extend toward a bright opening at the right of centre. Tiny standing figures near that opening offer another scale. The geometry makes the station feel large even where the portraits cover much of its structure.

sections.heading: A related cinematic idea
sections.body: In the official press notes, Campanella discusses the relationship between small people, enormous architecture and close views of eyes. That statement concerns his filmmaking approach. It offers a useful comparison with this poster, without proving that he personally designed its station-and-portrait arrangement.

regions.question: Which edge carries your eye deepest into the station?

regions.label: Distant figures
regions.summary: Two small silhouettes make the station measurable.

sections.heading: A minor but useful scale
sections.body: Small upright figures stand near the bright vanishing area behind the central woman. They are much smaller than the three principal portraits. Their narrow dark marks remain visible because the surrounding light is unusually clear and relatively free of surface detail.

sections.heading: Two kinds of looking
sections.body: You can read the large faces for expression, while the distant figures mainly explain space. This difference lets one poster combine psychological closeness with architectural distance. It does not require the tiny figures to be identifiable named characters.

regions.question: Would you still recognise the station’s size if these silhouettes were removed?

regions.label: Names above the image
regions.summary: Four surnames occupy a separate upper tier.

sections.heading: A different kind of introduction
sections.body: The upper wording presents actor surnames in pale capitals. These names introduce performers rather than characters. Their spacing distributes attention across the width before the portraits below establish a more unequal visual hierarchy of three main faces.

sections.heading: An invitation through recognition
sections.body: A viewer who already knows a performer may begin with the names, while another may begin with the faces. The design supports both routes. The presence of prominent billing demonstrates a marketing choice, not evidence of how audiences actually responded.

regions.question: Do you read a familiar name before looking at the face beneath it?

regions.label: Crime, mystery and love
regions.summary: A short sentence sets expectations across the bodies.

sections.heading: A compact bundle of genres
sections.body: The Spanish wording groups a crime, a mystery and a love, then refers to the secret of their lives. It suggests several ways to enter the film rather than explaining its full plot. The small pale line stretches horizontally across the dark jackets.

sections.heading: A pause before the title
sections.body: The campaign copy interrupts the portraits at a relatively quiet level before the much larger title below. It connects story promises to the name while leaving the faces visible. Its broad phrasing is an invitation, not a complete account of the film.

regions.question: Which promised element does the image itself make most visible?

regions.label: EL SECRETO DE SUS OJOS
regions.summary: Large white words occupy the lower darkness.

sections.heading: Read the Spanish wording
sections.body: El secreto de sus ojos is the Spanish title, officially presented in English as The Secret in Their Eyes. The possessive sus does not by itself specify a person’s gender. The large O shapes and extended lower word create a particularly open rhythm within the title.

sections.heading: Words linked to portraits
sections.body: A title about eyes encourages another look upward at the faces and their different gazes. That connection is visible even without knowing the plot. White letters also supply the clearest bright area in the otherwise dark lower third.

regions.question: Which face do the title’s words send you back to first?

regions.label: Small image beneath OJOS
regions.summary: A dim photographic fragment sits under the title.

sections.heading: A partially concealed detail
sections.body: A small, warm-toned photographic fragment is visible through the darkness beneath the title. Its scale and low contrast make it harder to resolve than the three upper portraits. Some of it is crossed by the large lettering, further interrupting recognition.

sections.heading: Keep uncertainty visible
sections.body: This reproduction does not justify a confident account of the fragment’s action or identities. Its role can still be studied: it adds another layer of information for close viewers while leaving the main title and upper faces immediately legible.

regions.question: Can you describe the shapes here without turning them into an assumed plot event?

regions.label: Director and release marks
regions.summary: A gold director line precedes the fine credits and logos.

sections.heading: A quieter final hierarchy
sections.body: Juan José Campanella’s name appears in a narrow gold line beneath the title area. The smallest billing and production logos occupy the bottom edge. These levels complete the poster’s information, but their fine lettering should not be expanded from an indistinct scan.

sections.heading: Practical identities at the edge
sections.body: The lower marks identify the production and release ecosystem after the portraits and title have attracted attention. Their small scale keeps the composition focused, but also means a visitor needs enlargement or an accessible transcript to study them closely.

regions.question: Which lower information remains readable when you view the whole sheet at once?

sources.title: The installed poster edition
sources.summary: The reproduced edition is the evidence for visible wording, layout, marks and colour relationships. Translations and visual interpretations are supplied by Poster Atlas.

sources.title: Sony Pictures Classics: official press notes
sources.summary: The synopsis and cast identify Espósito and Irene; Campanella’s director comments discuss memory, architecture and close views of eyes. The document concerns the film, not a confirmed poster-design intention.

rows.meaning: The Secret in Their Eyes; the official English film title.

connections.label: Depth through scale
connections.title: Three figures establish three distances
connections.text: The large man at left, smaller central woman and turned seated man make the station feel deeper than a flat portrait row.

connections.label: A red centre
connections.title: One jacket catches the warm light
connections.text: The red jacket creates a concentrated accent within the gold interior and dark suits.
